title: Impact of Meta AI-Generated Corrective Feedback in the Writing Classroom: Effects on L2 Writing Linguistic Errors
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether Meta AI-generated corrective feedback can reduce grammatical errors in L2 English writing, and whether different feedback types—direct, indirect, and metalinguistic—differ in effectiveness. The paper frames the problem as a gap in research on Meta AI integrated with WhatsApp for corrective feedback in writing instruction, especially for reducing morphological, syntactic, and orthographic errors.

The intervention involved three experimental sections using Meta AI through WhatsApp and one comparison section receiving teacher feedback. Section A received direct corrective feedback, Section B indirect corrective feedback, and Section C metalinguistic corrective feedback; Section D served as the control/comparison group with teacher-provided feedback. Students wrote short compositions regularly over a 12-week period, submitted drafts via WhatsApp, received feedback according to their assigned condition, revised digitally, and then rewrote the corrected text by hand. Outcomes were based on pretest/posttest writing tasks scored for linguistic errors by two doctoral raters.

Participants were 227 first-year undergraduate university students in India, aged 20 to 23, studying English in an English-medium context. The study was conducted at a single university, with the researcher serving as instructor for all groups. Although the paper mentions random sampling to select sections, it explicitly states that purposeful sampling was used to assign the four sections to groups, so the design is not a true randomized controlled trial.

The main conclusion is that all groups improved from pretest to posttest, but the metalinguistic Meta AI group showed the largest reductions in linguistic errors, especially syntactic errors. The authors argue that AI-generated metalinguistic feedback is more effective than direct or indirect AI feedback and more effective than teacher feedback in this context. However, the study does not report motivation outcomes, does not involve high-school students, and does not present the kind of 25-vs-25 randomized ChatGPT writing trial described in the retrieval topic. It therefore does not match the alleged high-school motivation RCT and should not be treated as evidence for that study description.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a comparative pretest-posttest intervention study with multiple groups and reported inferential statistics, but it is not a true randomized controlled trial. Students were randomly sampled into the study, yet intact sections were then purposively assigned to conditions, creating substantial risk of selection bias and making the design closer to a quasi-experiment with serious reporting inconsistencies.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests improvement in writing-error outcomes, especially for Meta-linguistic feedback, but impact magnitude is unclear because no defensible standardized effect size for the focal intervention is reported and the outcome metric is limited to error counts rather than broader writing quality. Any very large effect claimed in prior synthesis would not be supported by the original statistics presented here.

interventions.use_case: Meta AI delivered direct, indirect, and metalinguistic corrective feedback on students' English compositions submitted through WhatsApp, with outcomes based on reduction in morphological, syntactic, and orthographic writing errors.
Meta AI was used as an AI writing support tool for EFL undergraduates to analyze short compositions and provide grammar-focused feedback for revision and rewriting.
WhatsApp functioned as the mobile delivery platform through which students submitted drafts, received Meta AI feedback, and resubmitted revisions during the 12-week intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports reductions in writing errors from pretest to posttest across all groups, with the largest gains in the Meta-Linguistic Feedback group (Section C, n=58). For Section C, mean morphological errors decreased from 6.19 to 5.01, syntactic errors from 8.72 to 5.72, and orthographic errors from 6.96 to 5.14 over 12 weeks. However, no standardized writing-quality score, no between-group posttest-adjusted contrast, and no credible standardized effect size for writing performance were reported; the paper reports RM-ANOVA statistics such as a group effect F(3,223)=12.532, p<0.001, partial eta-squared=0.424 and a three-way interaction F(6,48)=2.532, p=0.033, partial eta-squared=0.240.
finding.measure: Counts of morphological, syntactic, and orthographic errors in 300-word English compositions at pretest and posttest
finding.effect_size: partial eta-squared=0.424 for group main effect; partial eta-squared=0.240 for three-way interaction; no standardized between-group effect size for writing reported
